lesson.title: Playing to Your Strengths: Signature Strengths and Their Use
lesson.summary: Signature strengths are the character traits most central and authentic to a particular person, and deliberately using them, not just possessing them, is linked to greater well-being.
lesson.body:
Alongside launching positive psychology as a field, Martin Seligman and psychologist Christopher Peterson set out to build something psychology had never quite had: a systematic classification of human strengths and virtues, deliberately conceived as something like a positive counterpart to clinical systems built to catalog what can go wrong with a person. Their 2004 project, published as Character Strengths and Virtues, organized twenty-four measurable character strengths, among them curiosity, kindness, honesty, humor, and persistence, under six broader virtues: wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance, and transcendence.

In this framework, everyone possesses all twenty-four strengths to some degree, but most people have a smaller number that feel distinctly like "them": strengths that get used often, that feel energizing rather than effortful to use, and that show up as a core part of how a person understands their own identity. Peterson and Seligman called these signature strengths.

Research has tested a fairly specific claim beyond simply identifying these strengths: does deliberately using a signature strength in a new way actually change how a person feels. In studies of positive psychology exercises, participants who identified a signature strength and were asked to use it in some new way each day for a week reported increased happiness afterward, an effect that in at least one widely cited study persisted for months. As with the gratitude research discussed earlier, it is worth being honest that positive psychology intervention research overall presents a mixed and still developing picture, with some effects smaller or less durable than early studies suggested, so these findings should be read as encouraging rather than as settled certainty.

Signature strengths connect naturally to well-being and resilience. They give a person a concrete, individualized resource to draw on, rather than a generic prescription for feeling better, and they can function specifically as something to lean on during hard times, one part of what may help explain why some people adapt more readily than others to the same difficult circumstance.
